progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: From b01: mutation is a change in base sequence; inside a gene it makes a new allele; it starts in one cell; a mutagen is something that harms DNA (named, not explained). From B4: complementary pairing (A with T, C with G), two strands, each a template; copying is accurate but not perfect; most errors are proofread and repaired. From B6b and B6c: codons are groups of three bases read in order. From B5a: a chromosome is one long DNA molecule. Year 11 Physics is not assumed: the electromagnetic spectrum and ionising are introduced with plain meanings.
progression.startsWith: A named agent raises the chance of a DNA change. The video opens: Every sunny day, ultraviolet light from the Sun damages the DNA in your skin cells, many times over in each exposed cell. Yet almost all of that damage never becomes a mutation.
progression.stopsAfter: distinguishing a mutagen (an agent that raises the chance of a DNA change) from a mutation (the change itself); explaining that damage to a base becomes a permanent mutation when it is copied before it is repaired, and that a wrongly rejoined break or inserted viral DNA can also make a lasting change, so exposure is a risk, not a guarantee; saying that UV, X-rays and gamma rays are electromagnetic radiation; explaining that UV is not ionising and joins neighbouring thymines into a dimer that distorts the DNA, mainly in skin cells; explaining that X-rays and gamma rays are ionising, break DNA strands directly and through free radicals, can cause large changes when breaks rejoin wrongly, and reach deep cells including those that make eggs or sperm; explaining three chemical routes; explaining naturally occurring mutagens and that natural does not mean harmless; applying this to an unseen UV against X-ray comparison and to the UV yeast data, separating survival from mutation.
progression.nextLesson: what one changed base can do to a protein (route entry bio-m6-b03), then chromosomal mutations (bio-m6-b04).

teaching.task: What does a mutagen physically do to DNA, and why doesn't every exposure end in a mutation?
teaching.causalExplanation: Causes: why UV isn't a mutation (it's an agent, 2); why base damage becomes permanent after copying (the wrong base gets its own partner, 3); why exposure is a risk (more damage, more chances that some is copied before repair or repaired wrongly, 4); why UV mainly affects skin (low penetration, 5); why UV mainly kinks rather than breaks (not enough energy to ionise; it bonds neighbouring thymines, 5); why X-rays break strands (ionising, directly and via free radicals, 6) and why a misjoined break needs no copying step to become a lasting change (6); why X-rays matter for eggs and sperm (deep penetration, 6); how each chemical causes an error (mimic, change, squeeze between, 7); why natural sources are mutagenic (same mechanisms, or inserted viral DNA, 8); the three routes to a lasting change (9).
teaching.conversationalApproach: sunlight on skin poses the question (damage every day, almost none becomes a mutation); one strand board shows every mechanism acting on the same DNA: the repair race for a damaged base, UV's dimer kink, X-ray breaks and free radicals, three chemical routes, and natural sources including inserted viral DNA; a mutagen board builds row by row into a summary with the three routes to a lasting change. Two exam questions follow with brief feedback.
teaching.openingDecision: UV damages the DNA in your skin cells every sunny day, yet almost all of it never becomes a mutation. So what exactly does UV do to DNA, what do X-rays and some chemicals do differently, and why doesn't damage always become a mutation?
teaching.understandingCheck: 11a: compare how UV and X-rays increase the risk of mutation in human cells, and which cells each is likely to affect. Answer: both damage DNA and neither guarantees a mutation; UV is not ionising and forms thymine dimers (wrong bases when copied), mainly in skin cells; X-rays are ionising and break strands (directly and via free radicals), and wrongly rejoined breaks lose or swap pieces, in cells throughout the body. Crossed mistake: "UV and X-rays damage DNA in exactly the same way". 11c: the site's UV yeast data (0, 15, 30, 60, 120 s; 142, 98, 61, 24, 5 colonies): describe the relationship and assess the conclusion that UV increased the mutation rate. Answer: longer exposure, fewer colonies, steepest at first; not supported, because counts measure survival, not mutation. Crossed mistake: "fewer colonies = more mutations". Each ends "Pause here to answer." with a 10 s countdown; each card stays on screen during and after the countdown.
teaching.curriculumScope: Syllabus (2017, BIO12-13, programme/syllabus/bio-2017-y12.json, B6-IQ1-01, p 51): "explain how a range of mutagens operate, including but not limited to: electromagnetic radiation sources; chemicals; naturally occurring mutagens". Point mutation names and protein effects are b03; chromosomal mutations b04; somatic against germ-line effects and cancer b05.

design.visualSystem: One strand board throughout: b01's SlimStrand drawn larger as a short double strand, on which each mechanism acts (DimerKink for a thymine dimer, StrandBreak for a gap with frayed ends, a notched rung end for a base analogue, a coded blob attached to a base, a flat slab sliding between rungs, a dashed inserted viral segment). Bases are named only in small callouts. A mutagen board builds row by row from scene 5 to scene 8 in the right third (source plate thumbnail, what it does, typical result) and becomes scene 9's summary with its three-route bar. Painted plates for every real source: m6-uv-skin-v1.png, m6-xray-machine-film-v1.png, m6-shielded-source-v1.png, m6-granite-outcrop-v1.png, m6-mouldy-peanuts-v1.png, m6-virus-particle-v1.png, m6-uv-cabinet-v1.png. New coded items: RepairRace, SpectrumBar with an ionising line, the depth bar (a layered block, no body), the exposure slider. Reuse: the explainer kit (Plate, Callout, Mark, Countdown, HandText, DrawPath, scribbleEllipse, Enter), B6a's WrongChip, GreyTag, Cross, Cam, the coded lineGraph. No people.
design.transitionPlan: The sun and skin plate opens with a magnifier onto the strand board; the mutagen and mutation cards draw side by side; the repair race splits into repaired and copied-first paths; the strand widens for the exposure slider; the spectrum bar draws across the top for UV and stays for X-rays, while each mechanism acts on the same strand and fills one mutagen board row; the board fills the screen for the summary and its three-route bar; the memory lines write over the dimer and gap icons; each attempt clears the board and its feedback shrinks the card to a strip and builds the comparison or the graph one point at a time; the step chips and next chip close; scene crossfade with settle.
